subject: Banking
title: Climate Risk in Banking
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Climate Risk in Banking.

hook.text: Banks hold $4.6 trillion in loans to fossil fuel companies.

buildup.text: Climate risk hits banking two ways: physical risk from weather destroying assets, and transition risk from policy.

discovery.text: Regulators now require climate stress tests. Banks must prove they can survive if carbon taxes double or seas rise.

twist.text: Some banks profit from both sides. They fund renewable energy while continuing to finance oil drilling.

climax.text: Climate is not distant risk. It is current balance sheet risk.

punchline.text: $4.6 trillion in fossil fuel loans. Climate risk is already on the books.

quiz.question: What are climate stress tests for banks?
options: Assessments of how banks would survive climate-related financial shocks

details.summary: Banks face growing exposure to climate risk through loans to fossil fuel companies, mortgages on flood-prone properties, and investments in industries threatened by the energy transition, forcing them to integrate climate into risk models.
details.whyItMatters: Climate change threatens the value of trillions in bank assets. A bank holding mortgages in areas facing rising sea levels or loans to coal companies faces losses that traditional risk models never anticipated.
takeaways: Banks hold trillions in climate-exposed assets that may lose value
Regulators now require climate risk stress testing for major banks
Green bonds and sustainable finance are the fastest-growing segments

faq.question: How does climate change create financial risk for banks?
faq.answer: Physical risks like floods and wildfires destroy collateral backing loans. Transition risks mean fossil fuel assets lose value as regulations tighten. Both types of risk can cascade through bank portfolios in ways that are difficult to model.

faq.question: Are banks divesting from fossil fuels?
faq.answer: Major banks have made net-zero pledges, but fossil fuel lending remains substantial. The transition is gradual because immediate divestment would strand billions in existing loans. Banks are shifting new lending toward renewable energy.
